Paragraph:
Translation: I would consider it better for the sons of Dhrtarastra to kill me unarmed and unresisting, rather than fight with them.

Purport (Excerpt): It is the custom—according to ksatriya fighting principles—that an unarmed and unwilling foe should not be attacked. Arjuna, however, in such an enigmatic position, decided he would not fight if he were attacked by the enemy... All these symptoms are due to softheartedness resulting from his being a great devotee of the Lord.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Having completely exhausted his rationalizations and emotional defenses, Arjuna reaches the absolute breaking point. He abandons all survival instincts and will to fight.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: He verbally declares his intention to become a passive victim. He states he would rather be murdered unarmed on the battlefield than participate in the violence against his family.
Outcome/Resolution: Arjuna entirely surrenders his agency, choosing death over the psychological torment of executing his duty.

Mental_Health_Theme_Synonyms.helplessness: Complete loss of agency, Giving up

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Ahimsa (Non-violence, taken to an extreme and inappropriate degree resulting in self-destruction)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Arjuna's softheartedness, while a symptom of his purity as a devotee, is completely misplaced here. By choosing passive death over righteous combat, he is abandoning the specific duty (Svadharma) assigned to him by God, showcasing the paralyzing power of material affection.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: This verse is a textbook expression of passive suicidal ideation stemming from an impossible psychological bind. Arjuna cannot bear to kill his family, and he cannot bear the shame of fleeing. To escape this inescapable trap, he wishes for death. He desires to be killed 'unarmed and unresisting' to finally end the agonizing mental conflict.
